name: Camera lens distortion (portrait lens 85mm)
lead: Perspective distortion in photographs makes features nearest the lens look larger. A face photographed close up with a wide-angle lens makes the nose appear bigger relative to the rest of the face, while a telephoto lens used from farther away makes it appear smaller.[1]

Portrait photography references name roughly 85-135 mm (35 mm equivalent) as a good range for portraits, with 75-135 mm cited for head-and-shoulders shots, and note that very short lenses exaggerate the nose and shrink the ears.[1][2] In looksmaxxing communities, longer focal lengths and greater distance are discussed as ways to reduce this effect in photos.
No clinical or perception studies on this practice were found in the references used.

paras: Linear perspective is determined mainly by the camera's distance from the subject rather than by the lens itself; two shots from the same position have the same perspective geometry.[1] Wide-angle lenses are normally used close, and telephoto lenses from farther away, so the lens choice and the distance usually go together.[1]

Viewing distance also matters: viewing a wide-angle image from closer, or a telephoto image from farther away, reduces apparent distortion.[1] Extremely long lenses can flatten facial features excessively.[1]

card.summary: Using a longer lens from farther back to reduce nose and face distortion; the optics are well documented.

quick.overview:
Wide-angle lenses used up close enlarge features nearest the camera, such as the nose. Longer lenses, often cited as 85-135 mm, used from farther away flatten the effect.

The optics are described in photography references. No study has tested how this changes rated attractiveness.
quick.mechanism: Perspective is set mainly by camera-to-subject distance. A longer lens lets the photographer stand farther back while still framing the face, reducing relative size differences between facial features.
